findings.title: New function bypasses the file's documented aiosqlite.Connection convention
findings.problem: Global CLAUDE.md states: 'Everything else — style, structure, architecture — yields to the existing codebase's conventions: before introducing a new pattern, check how the same problem is solved elsewhere in the repo and follow that.' triggarr/db.py's own module docstring (lines 1-6) documents the established convention: 'All public functions accept an aiosqlite.Connection instead of a Path, so callers share a single long-lived connection.' Every other function in the file (grep-confirmed) follows this; count_history_for_item alone takes `db_path: Path` and opens a new blocking `sqlite3.connect(db_path)`.
findings.fix_hint: change signature to `async def count_history_for_item(db: aiosqlite.Connection, item_name: str) -> int` and use `await db.execute(...)` like the rest of the module
findings.why_it_matters: A blocking sqlite3 connection opened per call, separate from the app's shared aiosqlite connection, can stall the event loop if invoked from async code and sidesteps the single-connection lifecycle (migrations, locking) the rest of db.py depends on.

members.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation of item_name
members.problem: Global CLAUDE.md Security section (absolute) states: 'Never interpolate user input into SQL — parameterized queries only.' This function builds its query with an f-string: `f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM search_history WHERE item_name = '{item_name}'"`, instead of binding item_name with a `?` placeholder as every other item_name-touching query in this same file does (triggarr/db.py lines 427, 546, 734).
source_window: f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM search_history WHERE item_name = '{item_name}'"
members.why_it_matters: A single quote in item_name (e.g. a title like "Ocean's Eleven") breaks the query, and crafted input can alter its logic or exfiltrate data; the rest of db.py treats this exact field as needing parameterization, confirming it's considered untrusted.
members.fix_hint: use `conn.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM search_history WHERE item_name = ?", (item_name,))`

members.title: Item names containing an apostrophe make the query crash or return the wrong count, and the query is open to SQL injection
members.problem: item_name is placed directly into the SQL text inside single quotes with an f-string. Item names are media titles from Radarr, Sonarr and Lidarr, and many contain apostrophes ("Schindler's List", "Ocean's Eleven", "Grey's Anatomy"). For a title like that, the quote closes the SQL string early, so sqlite3 raises OperationalError (syntax error) and the function throws instead of returning a count. A crafted title such as `x' OR '1'='1` gets past the filter and returns the count for every row in the table. The function catches nothing, so the error reaches the caller. The same problem is also a SQL injection (CWE-89), which breaks the project's rule to use parameterized queries only.
source_window: f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM search_history WHERE item_name = '{item_name}'"
members.why_it_matters: The count fails at runtime for common real titles, and crafted titles can change what the query returns.
members.fix_hint: use a parameterized query: conn.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM search_history WHERE item_name = ?", (item_name,))

members.problem: `count_history_for_item` builds its query with `f"...WHERE item_name = '{item_name}'"`, splicing the caller-supplied `item_name` directly into the SQL string instead of using a bound parameter. Every other query builder in this same file (e.g. lines 522-564) interpolates only placeholder/column-structure strings and passes actual values through `params`/`?` placeholders, so this is a deviation from the file's own established, safe pattern.

members.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in count_history_for_item
members.problem: The new function builds a SQL query by interpolating `item_name` directly into the string with an f-string and wraps it only in single quotes, with no escaping or parameterization. Any caller that passes external or user-influenced data (e.g. a movie/show/album title originating from Radarr/Sonarr/Lidarr metadata, a search query, or a UI filter) as `item_name` can break out of the string literal and inject arbitrary SQL. Since Python's `sqlite3.execute()` runs a single statement, classic stacked-query writes are blocked, but UNION-based injection is fully viable here: the query selects exactly one column (`COUNT(*)`), so a payload like `x' UNION SELECT api_key FROM some_config_table -- ` would return attacker-chosen data as the 'count', and boolean/error-based blind injection can probe the rest of the schema. Every other query in this file uses aiosqlite with bound parameters (`?` placeholders and a params tuple), so this new function is inconsistent with the file's own established safe pattern as well as the project's explicit rule.
source_window: f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM search_history WHERE item_name = '{item_name}'"
members.why_it_matters: If this helper is ever wired to any caller-supplied or metadata-derived value (a title, a search term, a value from an external API response), an attacker-controlled string containing a single quote can alter the query's logic or exfiltrate data from other tables via UNION SELECT, directly contradicting the project's own 'parameterized queries only' rule and its established pattern elsewhere in this same file.
members.fix_hint: use a parameterized query: conn.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM search_history WHERE item_name = ?", (item_name,))

members.title: Parameterize item_name to prevent SQL injection and title lookup failures
members.problem: The f-string interprets item_name as SQL. Executing the added function against an in-memory fixture confirmed that "Schindler's List" raises OperationalError, while "' OR 1=1 --" counts every row instead of matching the supplied name. Existing inserts support these strings through bound parameters. No callers of the new helper were found, so external exploitability is not established, but its documented counting behavior is demonstrably broken.

members.title: New DB accessor bypasses the module's established async aiosqlite connection-injection pattern
members.problem: Every other public query function in triggarr/db.py takes an injected `db: aiosqlite.Connection` and is async. Examples are get_recent_searches (L445), get_search_history (L487), get_trackable_entries (L591), update_outcome_and_stats (L648) and get_dashboard_stats (L752), and callers in web/routes.py, search/engine.py and tracking.py pass in the shared connection. count_history_for_item is the only function that opens its own synchronous `sqlite3.connect(db_path)` from a path. It skips the app's single managed connection and anything set on it, such as the row_factory used by `row["cnt"]`-style access. If an async route or the scheduler calls it, it will block the event loop.
source_window: def count_history_for_item(db_path: Path, item_name: str) -> int:
members.why_it_matters: A second way to reach the database splits connection handling and brings blocking I/O into an asyncio daemon. Future callers will copy whichever pattern they see first.
members.fix_hint: make it `async def count_history_for_item(db: aiosqlite.Connection, item_name: str)` using `async with db.execute(...)` like get_search_history

members.title: Synchronous sqlite3 helper in an otherwise all-aiosqlite module would block the event loop and skip WAL/connection conventions
members.problem: Every other DB function in db.py takes a shared `aiosqlite.Connection` (opened with PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL / synchronous=NORMAL at scheduler.py:455-457). This one opens a new blocking `sqlite3.connect(db_path)` with the default 5s busy timeout. If a FastAPI route or the async scheduler calls it, the event loop stalls during a full COUNT over search_history. I found no index on item_name in the schema near db.py:322, so this is a table scan that grows as history accumulates. It can also wait up to 5s on the writer lock. pending: confirm there is no item_name index and that a future caller is async.
